stateData.name: North Carolina
stateData.incomeTaxDesc: Flat 3.99% on other taxable income (pensions, 401k withdrawals)
stateData.propertyTaxNote: Low (0.66% effective rate — well below national average)
stateData.story: Flat 3.99% on other income, paired with a very LOW property tax rate of 0.66% (well below national median). Favorable overall retirement picture with zero tax on Social Security.
stateData.summary: North Carolina does not tax Social Security benefits at the state level (deducted on Form D-400 Schedule S). As of 2026, North Carolina enacted a simplified flat personal income tax rate of 3.99% across all taxable income, down from prior years. While North Carolina taxes private pensions, 401(k) distributions, and IRAs at this 3.99% flat rate, the state offsets this with a very low effective property tax rate of 0.66%—one of the lowest in the eastern United States. Qualifying low-income seniors aged 65+ can also claim the Elderly or Disabled Property Tax Homestead Exclusion.
stateData.aeoDirectAnswer: Social Security is 100% tax-free in North Carolina. The state taxes other retirement income at a modest flat rate of 3.99%, while offering a very low 0.66% effective property tax rate, creating an advantageous overall retirement environment.
stateData.otherRetirementTaxDesc: Flat 3.99% on 401(k), IRA, and private pension distributions.
stateData.propertyTaxDesc: 0.66% effective rate — well below national average, with homestead exclusions for qualifying seniors.
stateData.takeaway: Low 3.99% flat tax on pensions combined with a 0.66% property rate provides excellent cost predictability.

faqs.q: Is Social Security taxed in North Carolina?
faqs.a: No. North Carolina does not levy state income tax on Social Security benefits. You deduct your federal taxable benefits on Form D-400 Schedule S.

faqs.q: What tax rate does North Carolina charge on pensions and 401(k)s?
faqs.a: North Carolina applies a flat income tax rate of 3.99% on taxable pension distributions, 401(k) withdrawals, and traditional IRAs.

faqs.q: Do seniors get property tax relief in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Yes. North Carolina offers the Elderly/Disabled Exclusion, which excludes either $25,000 or 50% of the appraised value of a permanent residence (whichever is greater) for qualifying homeowners aged 65+ who meet income requirements.

otherStates.story: The cleanest 'no state tax anywhere' story. Florida levies zero personal income tax on Social Security, pensions, 401(k)/IRA distributions, or wages. Coupled with a moderate 0.78% effective property tax rate, retirees keep more of their fixed income.
otherStates.summary: Florida does not tax Social Security benefits at the state level. In fact, Florida has no personal income tax at all under Article VII, Section 5 of the Florida Constitution. Retirement income from all sources—including traditional 401(k) and IRA withdrawals, private pensions, government pensions, and investment earnings—is completely free from state income tax. Homeowners face a moderate effective property tax rate of 0.78%, and permanent residents can shield up to $50,000 of home value through Florida's Homestead Exemption.

faqs.q: Is Social Security taxed in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida does not tax Social Security benefits. Florida has no state personal income tax, so all Social Security payments are 100% exempt from state taxes.

faqs.q: Are pensions and 401(k) withdrawals taxed in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida levies zero state income tax on private pensions, public pensions, 401(k) withdrawals, traditional IRA distributions, or capital gains.

faqs.q: How high are property taxes for retirees in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida's statewide effective property tax rate is approximately 0.78%, which is below the national average. Florida also offers a Homestead Exemption shielding up to $50,000 of assessed home value for permanent primary residents.

otherStates.story: No state income tax on Social Security or retirement withdrawals, but property tax is 1.40% (one of the higher rates in the country). 'No SS tax, but don't assume zero property tax' — retirees who own homes face higher local property tax bills.
otherStates.summary: Texas does not tax Social Security benefits at the state level. Under the Texas Constitution (Article VIII, Section 24-a), the state bans personal income tax, meaning Social Security, pensions, 401(k) distributions, and IRAs are 100% state income tax-free. However, Texas funds public services largely through property taxes, resulting in an effective rate of 1.40%—among the higher rates in the US. Texas offers significant property tax relief for seniors, including an over-65 school tax ceiling (freeze) and additional residence homestead exemptions.
otherStates.aeoDirectAnswer: Social Security retirement benefits are 100% exempt from Texas state income tax. Texas has zero state personal income tax on all retirement income, though homeowners pay an effective property tax rate of 1.40% (offset by senior homestead exemptions).
otherStates.otherRetirementTaxDesc: 0% on pensions, 401(k) withdrawals, IRAs, and investment income.
otherStates.propertyTaxDesc: 1.40% effective rate — higher than average, but Texas provides an over-65 school tax freeze.
otherStates.takeaway: Zero income tax on benefits, but factor in higher property taxes when planning retirement housing.

faqs.q: Is Social Security taxed in Texas?
faqs.a: No. Texas does not tax Social Security benefits. Under the Texas Constitution, the state imposes zero personal income tax on Social Security or any other income.

faqs.q: Does Texas tax other retirement income like 401(k) or pensions?
faqs.a: No. All forms of retirement income—including 401(k) withdrawals, traditional IRA distributions, private pensions, and government annuities—are free from Texas state income tax.

faqs.q: Do seniors get property tax relief in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. Texas homeowners aged 65 and older receive an additional $10,000 homestead exemption on school district taxes and can 'freeze' their school property tax amount so it never increases above the ceiling established in their 65th year.

otherStates.name: California
otherStates.incomeTaxDesc: Progressive up to 13.3% on other retirement income (401k, pensions, investments)
otherStates.story: California does NOT tax Social Security specifically, but has a progressive income tax up to 13.3% on OTHER retirement income (pensions, 401(k) withdrawals, investment gains) — a crucial nuance retirees must know.
otherStates.summary: California does not tax Social Security benefits at the state level—benefits are fully deductible on California Form 540 (Schedule CA 540). However, California maintains the highest top marginal income tax rate in the country (up to 13.3%, or 14.4% including Mental Health Services tax on income over $1M) on OTHER retirement income. Traditional 401(k) distributions, traditional IRA withdrawals, corporate pensions, and capital gains are fully taxed as ordinary income at progressive state rates. On the real estate front, Proposition 13 limits base property tax increases to 2% annually, keeping the statewide effective property tax rate at 0.70%.
otherStates.aeoDirectAnswer: Social Security benefits are completely exempt from California state income tax. However, California taxes other retirement income—including 401(k) withdrawals, pensions, and investments—at progressive state rates reaching up to 13.3%, while property tax averages 0.70% under Prop 13.
otherStates.otherRetirementTaxDesc: Taxed as ordinary income at progressive rates from 1% up to 13.3%.
otherStates.propertyTaxDesc: 0.70% effective rate — protected by Prop 13, which caps annual assessed value increases at 2%.
otherStates.takeaway: SS is 100% safe, but diversified retirement portfolios face top-tier state income tax brackets.

faqs.q: Is Social Security taxed in California?
faqs.a: No. California completely exempts Social Security retirement, disability, and survivor benefits from state income tax. You subtract federal taxable benefits on California Schedule CA (540).

faqs.q: Does California tax 401(k) and pension income?
faqs.a: Yes. While Social Security is exempt, California taxes distributions from traditional 401(k)s, traditional IRAs, and private pensions as regular taxable income at rates from 1% up to 13.3%.

faqs.q: How does California Proposition 13 help retirees with property taxes?
faqs.a: Proposition 13 caps property tax at 1% of assessed value at purchase and limits annual inflation increases to a maximum of 2% per year. This keeps long-time homeowner property tax bills modest (averaging 0.70% effective rate statewide).
